I played a ridiculous amount of Dark Days Ahead, but The Last Generation seems like exactly what I was looking for instead. I love that most of my usual, high-powered sensibilities from CDDA have no place here. That first winter was pretty dicey, I will admit. Had to survive on horse milk, gummy bears, and the empty calories of hope, but after a year in-game spread over 160 hours of playtime, I'm finally feeling confident. The self-replicating chickens I've collected in my backyard are like a godsend, and this new layer of rat fur I've grown means my wind-powered evac shelter can be a walk-in freezer all year round (just as soon as I find more air conditioners.) The crops are coming in well. This next batch of pumpkin sugar will get me all the fruit leather I need to pull up stakes and start adventuring for real...maybe make a summer home out of that research facility just past the tree line. It's good to own land...

I was on walking home at night in a full plate armor just looted from a mansion and encountered a super soldier ant. I ran from it and thought I got away, but it found me again. It threw me away and I wielded my 9mm and unloaded a full magazine on it as it bit and grabbed me. It survived the salvo and I wielded my bronze sword and started bashing it while it dragged me away. Finally it let go of me and dispersed, I patched up my wounds a bit and started heading home. Not long until I encountered another one, knowing running would be futile I engaged and swung towards it while it dragged me away. After a while I was so wounded I could no longer hold my sword. Being dragged I took my exacto knife and cut away. After a while I could not hold it either and started yelling and punching it with my bare fists. I don't know what worked, but it let go and and fled and I could make some distance between us. With a broken arm, and almost dead I disinfected and bandaged, walking home for the second time. I managed to go for quite a bit, and thought I'd managed to make it, but encountered a normal soldier ant. Weak and unarmed I tried running but could not get away, the soldier and engaged and killed me in a few bites. What an amazing game!

First of all: game is FREE. You literally dont need to BUY IT. Just play a little before, then choose to buy or not. Second: BN is just better. You might be looking for some kind of "serious" experience, but it's impossible to achieve without improving and expanding the mechanics, deep rethinking, and a lot of work. That's not the case here. Here, everything negative is simply cranked up to the max, a bunch of stuff is cut out, and it's taught as something good, as some kind of useful work. TLG attempts to carve out a niche between the hyper-realistic, often overburdened simulation of modern DDA and the fast-paced, arcade-style action of BN. However, by trying to strip away the "tedium" of DDA while maintaining a hardcore survival experience, TLG ends up caught in a severe identity crisis. It frequently discards the depth of the original game only to replace it with artificial difficulty, clunky mechanics, and a sterile modding ecosystem. The Destruction of Combat and Stamina Management TLG actively discourages engaging with its combat systems through heavy-handed nerfs. Armor encumbrance penalties have been drastically increased, particularly for rigid armor. Classic "Survivor gear" has been nerfed and reclassified mostly as soft armor, meaning it fails to absorb serious damage. Attempting a heavily armored melee build results in massive penalties to dodge and attack speed, forcing players into fragile "glass cannon" builds where a single mistake is fatal. Shooting has become highly unreliable. The developer introduced a randomized variance (+/-) to hit calculations that leans heavily negative. Unlike DDA, where proper aim and recoil management guarantee a hit, TLG forces misses through pure RNG unless your Perception stat is astronomically high (18-20+). Stamina depletes at an absurd rate. A few swings of a heavy weapon or a short sprint will leave your character completely exhausted, turning encounters into inescapable death spirals. Regression of Complex Systems Instead of refining DDA's mechanics, TLG often rolls them back to outdated, primitive versions. In Modern DDA features a logical, science-based mutation system using primers and catalysts. TLG reverts this to the old arcade system: chugging mutagen from a flask. Because of the added "impurities" mechanic, drinking more than one mutagen a day leads to entirely random, often negative mutations, turning character development into a save-scumming casino. The removal of the Exodii faction completely destroys the narrative and quest-driven progression of acquiring bionics. Instead of trading and interacting with a cyborg faction, players are forced back to the archaic and uninspired mechanic of dissecting shocker zombies with a scalpel to randomly harvest high-tech implants. Artificial Tedium and Unbalanced Survival The attempt to remove the "cozy apocalypse" has resulted in a game that feels like a grueling chore rather than a rewarding challenge. The spawn rate for useful items has been nerfed to levels reminiscent of DDA's hardcore "No Hope" mod. Breaking into multiple safes only to find them completely empty is a common occurrence. This doesn't increase difficulty; it merely artificially inflates playtime by forcing endless grinding through empty houses. The metabolism rebalance is highly volatile. A character can eat a few high-calorie meals and, within a short in-game period (or after a nap), suddenly gain the "Morbidly Obese" trait. Losing this weight is incredibly difficult, and the resulting stamina penalties render the character nearly unplayable. Natural healing and bandage recovery rates have been slowed to an absurd degree. Even with regenerative mutations, players are forced to sit in a base reading books for days or risk venturing out with half their HP. Lighting fires for warmth or distraction now requires specific kindling. A simple fire in a house will often extinguish itself, adding unnecessary micro-management to a previously intuitive action. Technical Failures and the Solo-Dev Bottleneck As a hard fork maintained essentially by one person (Worm Girl), TLG suffers from severe infrastructure and stability issues. The most critical tool for any Cataclysm player—the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Cataclysm (HHG)—does not support TLG. Because recipes and stats have been rewritten since the March 2024 split, looking up information on the DDA wiki will constantly mislead you. Players are forced to read the raw GitHub code to understand the game. TLG breaks compatibility with 90% of modern DDA mods. Massive content overhauls like Magiclysm or Mind Over Matter are unsupported. Furthermore, the developer removed many of DDA's in-repo mods because they cannot maintain them alone. You are locked into a sterile, vanilla-only experience. To save on performance, neutral NPCs no longer require food, water, or sleep. This invisible crutch turns wandering NPCs into self-sustaining terminators, entirely breaking the immersion of a "realistic survival simulator." Despite this shortcut, their combat AI remains notoriously bad. Starter quests are not balanced around the player's weakened state. Early Hub-01 missions frequently spawn surrounding the objective with Hulks and evolved predators, making them mathematically impossible to complete for a fresh character. Artificial tileset ban Original DDA repository purged the immensely popular DeadPeople (UndeadPeople) tileset years ago over strict, puritanical copyright concerns. TLG inherited this exact mindset and went further, altering sprite mappings in a way that breaks third-party DeadPeople ports entirely. However, the Bright Nights (BN) fork proves that this restriction is completely unnecessary. BN has seamlessly maintained and supported DeadPeople natively for years. The sky hasn't fallen, the repository hasn't been sued into oblivion, and the players are happy. TLG's refusal to support the community's favorite tileset is an entirely self-imposed limitation. The situation highlights a broader issue with TLG's solo-development approach. Instead of accommodating community workarounds (as DDA players did by downloading DeadPeople via third-party repos), TLG’s diverging codebase actively burns the bridge. It dictates not just how you play the game, but exactly how it must look, isolating players who simply want a readable screen. If a player wants fast-paced, sci-fi action without the burden of micro-management (like nested containers), BN does it infinitely better, offering a stable engine and mech-building fun. If a player wants an incredibly deep, customizable, and realistic simulation, the original Dark Days Ahead remains unmatched due to its massive daily updates and vast modding community. TLG is stuck in a frustrating limbo. It retains the clunky inventory management of DDA but removes the rewarding simulation depth, and it attempts the hardcore focus of BN but ruins the combat pacing with excessive stamina drain and RNG penalties. It is a compromised, heavily restricted experience that demands much but offers very little in return. PS And also, you're going to laugh, but the female developer made the cars practically out of crystal, dumped a bunch of huge rocks in the fields and a ton of wrecked cars on the roads. And the most interesting part is that the cars became completely uncontrollable. Until your driving skill reaches 4 or higher, even at a speed of 30 km/h you will have massive problems with the handling, and the car absolutely won't obey you.

Do I like this game? Yes. I'm giving it a thumbs up because of that- but I like the game despite itself. Now let me rant for a *bit* here. It has the worst UI and controls I've experienced since Dwarf Fortress and Nethack. That's bad. Like *real* bad. Better contextual menus, better mouse support, more hidden mechanic explanations, more *anything* to explain what all the things do and what you need to be doing to do all the things would be really *really* great- and not just pages of text tucked in an encyclopedia, just little contextual hints (that you can turn off after you know what you're doing!) would make all the difference. Centralize more menus so you can look up things about your character/items more easily... there are like 8 different menus all mapped to 12 different keys to look up 20 different bits of information instead of, you know, a single character or item menu with actual tabs- and no, not that one character menu that has fake "tabs" all on the same page that you have to play a separate minigame to navigate- that's also bad and *still* lacks character info. Make better groupings in menus for making selections for actions you want to do, add categories to the ? contextual keybinds menu. Nuke most of the default keybinds and keep keybinds for important things, for example instead of '&' it should be 'c' for crafting, c for close doors can instead just open/close doors as a toggle with the open door key (which also probably shouldn't be 'o' and probably could just be wrapped into the 'a'ctivate menu)... there are so many more things like this in the game that could just be toggled or pulled into other existing systems. Lots of nonsensical keybinds too, my v key is for insert items into containers, p for Bionics, [ for Mutations, $ for sleep? Okay, I'll admit that @ for a character stats page *is* a nice touch. Also, I get that you can rebind things, but come on- most people will use the defaults and that's their first experience of the game. Make inventory sorting easier. Consolidate the '/' and 'g' menus- there should only be one "get/move items" menu and it should have the functionality of both since / doesn't handle containers super well (heck, maybe this should just be rolled into inventory tabs for inv vs nearby). Have containers be the top level of all inventories and open into new bag menus/tabs showing contents- not just mixed in randomly in places. Have a single separate "here is what you have equipped" menu with better controls/indicators of what things are ACTUALLY doing for you- all in one place! The { menu (yep, that's the keybind!) for body parts is practically useless since it lacks so much info and you can't do anything there. Add an option to blacklist all categories in one go so I can more easily make containers that are "No, really, I just want *this* in there" It's also buggy, I've encountered several errors that you just type ignore to keep going to and when I started I had to mess with the graphics settings a lot just to get the game to stop flickering. But you know what? Despite *ALL* that my constantly mutating extra large cold blooded alligator razor girl with bladed bionic fingertips wearing a crafted pink faux fur coat, a quilted gambeson, combat boots, an army helmet, a leather tail sleeve, and a long wool scarf for muzzle warmth is tearing through zombies with kung fu style dragon tail sweeping attacks and clawing monsters from another world in twain... once victorious she can then pulp their corpses into fine mushy oblivion so they never come back. Which is pretty f'ing rad. Simultaneously the best and worst game I've played in a while.

Great version of Cataclysm that is actually fun to play. Most of the negative reviews either complain about personal issues with the developer or about the game not being the exact version of Cataclysm they think would be perfect. You can look up the changes and even try them out for free by getting the fork from GitHub; it’s not like the changes are hidden. You can easily decide whether you like them before buying the version on Steam. Buying this is a way to support the developer and get your game updates through Steam. If you don’t want that, just try the free version first.

There are a lot of CDDA forks and recommended packs and this and that, but just like DF, if you want to give money to a beautiful use of your free time, this is where you do it for Cataclysm. Worm Girl's an extremely detail oriented dev, updates come out for this CONSTANTLY and you can feel the care for the crafted experience.

Yea I played this one a little bit. It's fine. Ignore the negative reviews by salty CDDA devs, they are mad that their toxic attiude towards fans has now come back to bite them in the @$$. They were the monopoly on "decent realistic survival cataclysm branch", and now with the introduction of CTLG, they are not. This fork is rough, and I said it as someone who has 1000s hours in CDDA and CBN. But not in the sense that it's bad, it's just harder than the other two, and you won't feel like a demigod among men anytime soon, but when you do, it would feel like you earned it. It would feel like you have torn that $h!t from the mouth of defeat and the gate of hell. It would make you proud (after it made you sweat and shiver countless times before that. I swear I spent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ MINUTES in real life for a turn in which I stupidly or carelessly put my character in precarious positions. But when I managed to get out of those by any means possible, the high I've got was incomparable to anything I've experienced in my gaming life so far. Buy it, play it. Or do it the other way around because Worm Girl is a chad who gave the world this gem for free on github. But no matter which way you go about doing it, just ignore the blatant negative reviews. It's a shame that a game as magical as Cataclysm got so much drama behind it, but that's life I guess.

I'm helplessly addicted to this game. I've tried to play other games and I can't, I just can't focus on anything but this quirky, tough all-apocalyspes survival game. Cataclysm: TLG and DDA both ask a lot from the player just to operate them, but they give so much back just in terms of how much freedom you have to attempt survival. Want to crash a car into a house and leave the stereo pumping loud as can be to attract the whole horde of zombies? Go for it. Then want to sneak out the back door and chuck a molotov in behind you? No problem. Now you can enjoy watching the house burn down and kill most of the zombies. If you can come up with a plan, this game will let you do it—provided you've figured out how the systems work to make it happen. Watch Worm Girl's youtube tutorials; they may be a little dated and from DDA, but they're still a great help!
